source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)

coverage.syllabus: Lubbers Fall 2026 IV.C Rulemaking: findings/reasons pp. 306–316; issuance/publication pp. 316–324

topics.title: § 5.6 — Findings, Reasons, Responses to Comments (pp. 306–316)
topics.description: Full Independent Insurers case, Texas APA vs federal APA and D.C., Auto Parts, Rodway, Ohio v EPA, Chenery, Workers Compensation hypothetical.

entries.title: Why reasons must accompany final rules
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Federal APA § 553(c) requires a concise general basis-and-purpose statement; some state APAs impose more explicit reasoned justification and responses to comments.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency needs to tell people why its rule makes sense, rather than simply saying it wants fairness.
entries.legalExplanation: Reason-giving promotes rationality, democratic accountability, substantive objections, and effective judicial review; degree of explanation varies across statutes.
entries.examApplication: Identify exact governing APA and timing, distinguish procedural adequacy from substantive merits.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume every state requires the same federal-style statement.

entries.title: Texas APA § 2001.033: heightened reasoned justification
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: For adopted rule Texas law demands clear, precise, logical reasoning including comment summary, factual basis, and reasons for disagreement. Failure of substantial compliance invalidates rule under § 2001.035(a).
entries.laymanExplanation: Texas agency must explain what evidence it relied on and why it disagreed with important opponents.
entries.legalExplanation: Requires (1) summary of comments, (2) factual restatement, (3) reasoned justification linked to evidence; looks beyond empty conclusion.
entries.examApplication: Assess each mandatory element against actual agency statement.
entries.examTrap: 'Better competition' as bare slogan may not establish logical connection.

entries.title: National Association of Independent Insurers v. Texas Department of Insurance, 925 S.W.2d 667 (Tex. 1996)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: No. Texas Supreme Court invalidated both rules for inadequate reasoned justification and reversed intermediate court; agency could try again with adequate explanation.
entries.laymanExplanation: An adopting order must state a clear logical connection between evidence and regulatory choice, summarize comments and explain rejection of significant objections under the Texas APA; generic pro-consumer labels are insufficient.
entries.legalExplanation: Agency conclusorily asserted previous denial unfair, without explaining why consideration as one factor necessarily anti-competitive; Rule 1003 simply said affordability improved without explaining disparate treatment of umbrella vs other tie-in coverage or multiple-vehicle pricing. Statute requires actual reasoning, not just abstract goals, public/courts must see logic. Dissent agreed Rule 1003 invalid but found Rule 1000 substantially compliant; criticized clause-by-clause overreach.
entries.examApplication: Assess actual text justifying each rule separately; discuss majority versus dissent's level of precision and judicial intrusion.
entries.examTrap: Do not say Texas court held banning blacklisting substantively illegal; it found procedural explanation insufficient.
entries.sourceRole: Opinion excerpt reproduced in assigned textbook
entries.facts: Texas Board of Insurance adopted Rule 1000, prohibiting underwriting denial based in whole or part on previous insurer's cancellation/refusal, and Rule 1003, restricting single-car/tied-coverage practices. Insurers attacked adoption orders for failure to satisfy Texas APA reasoned-justification requirements. Trial and intermediate courts upheld rules.
entries.issue: Did general claims of anti-competitiveness, blacklisting and fairness adequately justify these specific prohibitions under Texas APA § 2001.033?
entries.holding: No. Texas Supreme Court invalidated both rules for inadequate reasoned justification and reversed intermediate court; agency could try again with adequate explanation.
entries.reasoning: Agency conclusorily asserted previous denial unfair, without explaining why consideration as one factor necessarily anti-competitive; Rule 1003 simply said affordability improved without explaining disparate treatment of umbrella vs other tie-in coverage or multiple-vehicle pricing. Statute requires actual reasoning, not just abstract goals, public/courts must see logic. Dissent agreed Rule 1003 invalid but found Rule 1000 substantially compliant; criticized clause-by-clause overreach.
entries.rule: An adopting order must state a clear logical connection between evidence and regulatory choice, summarize comments and explain rejection of significant objections under the Texas APA; generic pro-consumer labels are insufficient.

entries.title: Independent Insurers majority versus partial dissent
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Majority demanded explanation of why even partial reliance on cancellation was unlawful, and why particular tie-ins were forbidden. Dissent accepted Rule 1000's logic as a whole under substantial-compliance standard.
entries.laymanExplanation: Does 'no blacklisting' explain why every use of prior denial is barred? Justices disagreed.
entries.legalExplanation: The dispute concerns procedural explanation stringency and risk courts substitute their policy views.
entries.examApplication: Discuss line between demanding explanation and doing agency policy analysis.
entries.examTrap: Dissent concurred in invalidating Rule 1003.

entries.title: Reason-giving as legitimacy vs administrative burdens
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Mashaw views reasons as treating people as rational participants entitled to evaluate policy; Frohnmayer warns small state agencies lack time, staff and ability to rationalize group intuitive choices.
entries.laymanExplanation: Explanations make government accountable, but small boards might not have staff to write detailed studies.
entries.legalExplanation: D.C. APA example lacks general written reasons requirement by deliberate local legislative choice; state laws vary.
entries.examApplication: Compare state requirements before invalidating rule.
entries.examTrap: Source presents academic policy debate, not federal universal exception.

entries.title: Federal APA § 553(c): concise general statement interpreted robustly
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Despite modest original language, federal courts require sufficiently explanatory basis and purpose to identify major policy issues and agency responses, not detailed treatment of every submission.
entries.laymanExplanation: A rule's justification can be concise, but must show why agency chose that policy and dealt with main objections.
entries.legalExplanation: Automotive Parts v Boyd rejected literal shallow reading of 'concise general'; courts need reviewable reasons rather than invent agency's rationale.
entries.examApplication: Identify the main contested tradeoff and what agency said about it.
entries.examTrap: No requirement to respond to every marginal comment or write trial-style fact findings.

entries.title: Automotive Parts & Accessories Association v. Boyd, 407 F.2d 330 (D.C. Cir. 1968)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Federal statement must let court see major policy issues raised in rulemaking and why agency resolved them as it did.
entries.laymanExplanation: Judges shouldn't reconstruct first rationale from mountains of raw comments.
entries.legalExplanation: Court gloss on § 553(c) debated as potentially inconsistent with Vermont Yankee.
entries.examApplication: Use where explanatory statement too cursory.
entries.sourceRole: Summarized in casebook Notes and Questions, not excerpted full opinion

entries.title: Significant comments require reasoned response
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Agency must consider and address material comments which, if true, could warrant changing rule; no duty to answer unsupported speculation or every small objection.
entries.laymanExplanation: A serious study showing your rule won't work requires answer; an irrelevant guess doesn't.
entries.legalExplanation: Rodway rule; Perez v Mortgage Bankers dictum; significance often intertwined with § 706(2)(A) arbitrary/capricious review.
entries.examApplication: Specify what commenter argued, relevance to statutory test, and agency response.
entries.examTrap: The obligation is not a numerical requirement to answer each of 2,520 comments.

entries.title: Rodway v. USDA, 514 F.2d 809 (D.C. Cir. 1975)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Agency's basis/purpose statement must explain reasoned reaction to significant problems raised by commenters.
entries.laymanExplanation: Consideration is not fulfilled by abstract justification that ignores concrete objections.
entries.legalExplanation: Reference case discussed in notes.
entries.sourceRole: Summarized in casebook Notes and Questions, not excerpted full opinion

entries.title: Ohio v. EPA, 603 U.S. 279 (2024) — comments and changed scope
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Supreme Court stayed cross-state NOx pollution plan after states covered shrank from 23 to 12 and EPA did not adequately address commenters' cost-effectiveness concern. Barrett dissent contested whether concern was raised with reasonable specificity.
entries.laymanExplanation: If half the states drop out, agency must explain whether emissions-control plan still makes economic sense when comment fairly raises it.
entries.legalExplanation: Majority says reasoned response missing; dissent says one ambiguous submission insufficient and error possibly harmless.
entries.examApplication: Explain opposing assessments of how specifically comment raised collapse in state coverage.
entries.examTrap: Don't assert agency must independently answer every vaguely hinted issue.
entries.sourceRole: Summarized in casebook Notes and Questions, not excerpted full opinion

entries.title: Ohio v EPA: significant-comment specificity disputed
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Majority treated submitted concern about reduced regulated states as important; dissent contested specificity and materiality of objection.
entries.laymanExplanation: Courts disagree whether the commenter clearly warned agency about later changed circumstances.
entries.legalExplanation: Provides sophisticated issue-preservation and comment-response illustration alongside arbitrary/capricious standards.
entries.examApplication: Show actual facts of comment and agency's changes.
entries.examTrap: Casebook note, not full opinion excerpt; no fabricated full brief.

entries.title: Chenery doctrine bars post hoc counsel justification
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Courts generally judge agency regulatory choices on contemporaneous reasons agency itself stated, not litigation rationalizations lawyers later propose.
entries.laymanExplanation: Government lawyers can't invent the agency's explanation after they're sued.
entries.legalExplanation: Chenery I principle ensures delegated policymaking authority exercised by agency rather than judicial reconstruction; legal interpretation nuances discussed in notes.
entries.examApplication: Compare basis/purpose text to later statutory deadline asserted solely in court.
entries.examTrap: Agency can potentially explain on remand; post hoc lawyers do not cure original decision.

entries.title: Reasons and arbitrary/capricious merits review overlap
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Courts often examine § 553(c) adequacy with § 706(2)(A) rational-connection review, but states with no statement duty complicate procedure-based claims.
entries.laymanExplanation: A bad explanation can be both a procedural failure and evidence decision wasn't rational.
entries.legalExplanation: Encino Motorcars linked basic rulemaking reason duty to ordinary arbitrary/capricious precedent; substantive agency record remains relevant.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish nature of challenge and available standard across federal, Texas, D.C.
entries.examTrap: Absence of a state written explanation statute does not automatically immunize substantively arbitrary action.

topics.title: § 5.7 — Issuance, Publication, Delayed Effectiveness (pp. 316–324)
topics.description: Federal Register/CFR, § 552 guidance posting, incorporation by reference, § 553(d) waiting period, midnight rules and Alvin pizza kitchen problem.

entries.title: Why rules must be published
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Publication gives regulated public access to binding law, opportunity to conform and means to hold agency accountable.
entries.laymanExplanation: You shouldn't be punished under a secret regulation no one can reasonably see.
entries.legalExplanation: Federal APA § 552(a)(1), FRA and state APA public inspection systems; legal enforceability often hinges on required public release or actual timely notice.
entries.examApplication: Ask publication medium, rule type, date, person's actual knowledge.
entries.examTrap: Unpublished guidance and binding substantive regulations face different statutory requirements.

entries.title: Federal Register Act and CFR
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: FRA 44 U.S.C. §§ 1501–1511 requires Federal Register workday publication for general applicability/legal effect rules and notices; CFR codifies applicable regulations in 50 subject titles.
entries.laymanExplanation: Federal Register announces a rule; CFR organizes operative regulations for easy reference.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook uses Panama Refining history of unavailable/missing executive petroleum orders as motivation.
entries.examApplication: Identify where binding regulation appears and effective date.
entries.examTrap: Publication and actual effective date are distinct.

entries.title: Federal APA § 552(a)(1) publication requirement
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Agencies must publish substantive rules of general applicability, applicable policy/interpretations of general applicability, and other enumerated matters in Federal Register; limited actual-and-timely notice exception.
entries.laymanExplanation: New legal obligations should be publicly announced before government invokes them against you.
entries.legalExplanation: Section § 552(a)(1)(D) expressly references both legislative rules and general policy/interpretations; qualification whether guidance qualifies sometimes disputed.
entries.examApplication: Classify bulletin general applicability or internal interpretive case-specific document.
entries.examTrap: Do not say every internal agency memorandum must appear in Federal Register.

entries.title: APA § 552(a)(1) versus (a)(2) guidance access puzzle
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: § 552(a)(1)(D) appears to demand general policy/interpretations in Federal Register, while § 552(a)(2)(B) requires public inspection/electronic availability for adopted interpretations not published there; secret (a)(2) precedent unavailable against party without actual timely notice.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency may not quietly rely on a hidden interpretive bulletin if statute required disclosure and party had no notice.
entries.legalExplanation: Courts draw uncertain lines, often construe (a)(1) narrowly for general applicability and significant public impact; Powderly criterion in notes.
entries.examApplication: Ask whether adopted statement is general rule or staff instruction, publication/inspection and actual/timely notice.
entries.examTrap: Don't assume only legislative rules trigger disclosure obligations.

entries.title: Powderly v. Schweiker, 704 F.2d 1092 (9th Cir. 1983)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Court narrowly interpreted which administrative interpretations have general applicability under § 552(a)(1)(D), considering clarification and significant impact.
entries.laymanExplanation: Not every agency legal explanation deserves full Federal Register announcement.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook flags potential tension with literal statute.
entries.examApplication: Apply guidance public impact.
entries.sourceRole: Summarized in casebook Notes and Questions, not excerpted full opinion

entries.title: Incorporation by reference under APA § 552(a)(1)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Agency may incorporate privately published standard by reference with Office of Federal Register Director's approval if material reasonably available; public access/copyright expense remains debated.
entries.laymanExplanation: Rule can point to industry safety manual instead of printing whole thing, but manual should be obtainable.
entries.legalExplanation: ACUS 2011–5 proposed read-only access; 2023 D.C. Circuit copyright decision ASTM v Public.Resource.org recognized certain noncommercial code sharing as fair use.
entries.examApplication: Ask accessibility, notice and permission to incorporate.
entries.examTrap: 'Reasonably available' is not equivalent to universal free online access under excerpted source.

entries.title: American Society for Testing & Materials v. Public.Resource.org, 82 F.4th 1262 (D.C. Cir. 2023)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Noncommercial distribution of incorporated-by-reference standards counted as fair use for copyright purposes in casebook treatment.
entries.laymanExplanation: A public-interest site might legally share materials that became law through regulation.
entries.legalExplanation: Not a replacement for § 552 incorporation requirements.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish copyright from APA compliance.
entries.sourceRole: Summarized in casebook Notes and Questions, not excerpted full opinion

entries.title: APA § 553(d): 30 days before legislative rule effectiveness
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: General federal rule becomes effective not earlier than 30 days after final publication; 1961 MSAPA generally 20 days after state official publication.
entries.laymanExplanation: Government typically gives regulated people preparation time after announcing final rule.
entries.legalExplanation: Designed for notice and chance to adapt; proposed rule notice is not sufficient substitute for FINAL publication.
entries.examApplication: Count from published FINAL rule, not NPRM.
entries.examTrap: A rule issued today usually cannot be enforceable tomorrow absent exception.

entries.title: Exceptions to 30-day delayed effect
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Immediate effectiveness permitted for substantive rules granting/recognizing exemption or relieving restriction (§ 553(d)(1)); interpretive rules and general policy statements (§ 553(d)(2)); or good cause found and published with rule (§ 553(d)(3)).
entries.laymanExplanation: Helpful or explanatory rules may take effect immediately; urgent burden rules need published real reason.
entries.legalExplanation: State 1961 MSAPA has imminent peril exception for 20-day wait. Check statute and scope; good cause must be stated in rule.
entries.examApplication: Classify rule and record existence of agency's contemporaneous good-cause finding.
entries.examTrap: Skipping 30-day period does not necessarily mean entire rule forever void; remedy may delay.

entries.title: Rowell v. Andrus, 631 F.2d 699 (10th Cir. 1980)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Final federal lease payment increase appeared Jan 5 with Feb 1 start, under 30 days; draft had appeared months earlier but court required time from final publication, postponed effective date rather than vacating substance.
entries.laymanExplanation: A proposed rule cannot start 30-day final rule clock.
entries.legalExplanation: Remedy can be delayed effectiveness, not wholesale vacatur.
entries.examApplication: Calculate dates precisely.
entries.sourceRole: Summarized in casebook Notes and Questions, not excerpted full opinion

entries.title: Rule delay often itself requires notice-and-comment
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Once binding rule promulgated, postponing effective date changes its legal effect and generally requires rulemaking; agencies can't simply impose blanket pause without statutory exception.
entries.laymanExplanation: A new President cannot always stop a signed rule by issuing a memo—moving start date can be another rule.
entries.legalExplanation: NRDC v NHTSA and Clean Air Council v Pruitt treated post-final delays as rulemaking and subject to rational explanation.
entries.examApplication: Apply to presidential transition/midnight rules.
entries.examTrap: Do not conflate withdrawing unfinalized documents with changing effective finalized regulation.

entries.title: Humane Society of United States v. USDA, 41 F.4th 564 (D.C. Cir. 2022)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Rule can be finalized by filing for public inspection at Office of Federal Register before Federal Register publication; new administration cannot simply retrieve it and treat as unissued.
entries.laymanExplanation: Filing at OFR may complete finalization even if publication comes later.
entries.legalExplanation: Source says limits earlier Kennecott practice allowing withdrawals.
entries.examApplication: Trace filing vs actual publication vs effective time.
entries.sourceRole: Summarized in casebook Notes and Questions, not excerpted full opinion

entries.title: Midnight rules: outgoing and incoming administrations
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Outgoing Presidents issue regulations late term; successors may withdraw documents not yet legally final or use proper procedures to delay/repeal. ACUS proposed 60-day legislative review window.
entries.laymanExplanation: Rules can race to finish before inauguration, while successor has limited legally compliant options to pause them.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook weighs democratic accountability and speed; limits to delaying existing regulations apply irrespective party.
entries.examApplication: Separate status pre-filing, filed, final published, effective and repeal procedure.
entries.examTrap: ACUS 2012–2 is recommendation, not statutory 60-day right.

problems.title: Federal 'concise' explanations and Vermont Yankee

problems.title: Madison Workers' Compensation Hospital Rates — textbook problem
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 315–316)
problems.prompt: Board adopted flat per-day rates for medical, surgery and intensive care using survey mean minus 10%, overlooking hospitals' differing complexities and comment requesting more study. Statement only noted average costs and cost containment; in litigation counsel claims statute compelled year-end completion. Should court remand under (i) federal APA, (ii) Texas reasoned-justification law, (iii) D.C. APA with no general written statement requirement? Consider Chenery, significant comments, rational connection, leave unsolved.

problems.title: Does secret guidance bind regulated parties?

problems.title: Incorporated standards and public access

problems.title: 30-day waiting-period and proper remedy

problems.title: Midnight rules and change of administration
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 322–323)
problems.prompt: How do unpublished but filed and final published regulatory actions differ regarding withdrawal, postponement and repeal under Kennecott, Humane Society and § 553?

problems.title: Alvin / grocery pizza kitchen Bulletin 260 and Rule 36 — textbook problem
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 306–324 (user-uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 323–324)
problems.prompt: Madison meat inspection: Secretary issued never-posted Bulletin 260 construing 'packing' to cover Alvin's central pizza kitchen, then inspectors demanded costly upgrades and penalties. Agency later used NPRM to adopt identical Regulation 36 effective immediately without explanation. Alvin challenges unpublished bulletin, immediate effect and asks delayed date until jurisdiction resolved. Analyze federal APA § 552(a), § 553(d), good cause, interpretive/legislative distinction, statutory coverage and 1961 MSAPA 20-day period—leave answer unsolved.
